version_history.subject: [PATCH] btrfs: keep unused block groups queued when a pass fails

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch addresses a potential issue in the btrfs file system where unused block groups can be leaked and lead to spurious ENOSPC errors. The problem occurs when an error is encountered while deleting unused block groups, causing them to be skipped and not re-queued for later processing. To fix this, the patch changes the logic of the deletion loop to break out of it when an error is encountered, rather than skipping the rest of the block groups. Additionally, it links the failing block group to a retry list at the individual failure sites, ensuring that it is not leaked.

review_comments.author: Qu Wenruo
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Qu Wenruo questioned which error caused a non-zero @ret value in the loop and suggested that the issue might be due to incorrect reserved space checking by inc_block_group_ro() checks.

Reviewer noted that the patch's approach of breaking out of the loop when ret != 0 may not be sufficient, as it delays error handling to the next iteration.
review_comments.raw_body:
Do have happen to know which error caused this non-zero @ret?

I did a quick glance into the loop, it looks like it's not that easy to 
get a non-zero @ret:

- inc_block_group_ro() failure
   @ret is reset to 0, so not this path.

- btrfs_zone_finish()
   I guess meta is not deploying zoned btrfs in production.

- btrfs_star_trans_remove_block_group()
   This can return -ENOSPC, especially considering we have just marked
   one bg read-only, thus even stealing from global rsv, we may still
   fail with ENOSPC here.

   Although I'd say, that means the inc_block_group_ro() checks are not
   doing the correct reserved space checking, and that may be the real
   problem.

- btrfs_remove_chunk()
   If it failed, the trans is already aborted.

---

Otherwise the handling looks correct to me, doing the proper handling on 
error, other than delaying it to the next iteration.

Thanks,
Qu

version_history.subject: [PATCH] mm/madvise: reclaim isolated folios if PTE restart fails

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch addresses a concurrency issue in the Linux kernel's madvise functionality. When MADV_PAGEOUT is used to collect isolated folios, a concurrent operation can remove or replace the PTE table while the lock is dropped, causing pte_offset_map_lock() to return NULL and bypassing reclaim_pages(). The patch routes this failure through the existing cleanup path, ensuring that any collected folios are reclaimed or put back. This fix prevents a situation where isolated folios remain off the LRU with elevated references.

review_comments.author: Gregory Price (author)
review_comments.summary: The author is addressing a concern about the testability of mm/ components, specifically the page allocator and other parts of memory management. The author has been exploring various testing mechanisms, including selftests, Usermode Linux (UML), userland VMA tests, and the Linux Test Project. They have found that selftests are limited and create maintenance burdens, but have made progress in using UML and userland VMA tests to stub out reclaim calls and demonstrate basic correctness for a combination of commands into the page allocator. The author is optimistic about making test-driven development feasible with the help of Large Language Models (LLMs).

Yes, in fact I used that as a start for exploring how I might make other
components testable the same way.

"Stubs... stubs everywhere"

There's basically 4 testing mechanisms i explored:

1) selftest
2) Usermode Linux (UML)
3) Userland stuff like VMA
4) Linux Test Project (for syscall and ABI testing)

selftests are really limited and actually create a maintenance burden,
they're not real unit tests and are highly dependent on the actual
machine configuration which is super annoying.

But, lets take the page allocator as an example.

The only piece of the page allocator that "should" (cough, simplifying
here a bit) be machine specific is zone and node configurations... but
I'm not convinced that this should require a full VM to unit-test.

(other caveat: obviously some things like RCU and interrupt contexts are
hard in userland, putting that aside for now).

We should be able to stub out the reclaim calls and at least demonstrate
basic correctness for a combinatrix of commands into the page allocator.

Anyway...

I've been looking at how to use the VMA and UML test infrastructure to
stub out even more of mm/ and generate these kinds of basic contract
tests.  So far I've found bugs in a few random corners, but nothing
critical or reachable as far as i can tell - so that's nice.

Have made it compilable with ASAN and Coverage

The harness itself turns into a decent fuzzer as well for basic stupid
logic conditions, which in turn allows coverage and LLM guided fuzzing
into an easier task for any random kernel dev to start engaging in.

> atm. May set the LLM on it though...

On Sat, Sep 12, 2026 at 07:08:32AM -0400, Gregory Price wrote:
> MADV_PAGEOUT collects isolated folios on a local list before reclaiming
> them after the PTE walk.  The reschedule path drops the PTE lock and then
> restarts the mapping with pte_offset_map_lock().

Is this reschedule path even necessary? It's pretty bloody sketchy.

I thought the modern approach (TM) was to not do cond_resched() and friends so
can we actually look at removing this?

>
> A concurrent operation can remove or replace the PTE table while the lock
> is dropped, causing pte_offset_map_lock() to return NULL.  Returning directly
> in that case bypasses reclaim_pages(), leaving the collected folios off the
> LRU with elevated references.
>
> Route the failure through the existing cleanup path so any isolated folios
> are reclaimed or put back.
>
> Simplest userland pseudo-code reproducer:
>
> p = mmap(PMD_SIZE, ANONYMOUS);
> touch_every_page(p, PMD_SIZE);
> parallel {
>    while (1) madvise(p, PMD_SIZE, MADV_PAGEOUT);
>    while (1) {
>        madvise(p, PMD_SIZE, MADV_DONTNEED);
>        touch_every_page(p, PMD_SIZE);
>    }
> }
>
> Reproduced in qemu trivially with some explicit widening of the race window.
>
> Fixes: b2f557a21bc8 ("mm/madvise: add cond_resched() in madvise_cold_or_pageout_pte_range()")
> Reported-by: sashiko-bot <sashiko-bot@kernel.org>

> +++ b/mm/madvise.c

This function is truly some of the absolute worst code I've read in
mm. Shocking.

>  restart:
>  	start_pte = pte = pte_offset_map_lock(vma->vm_mm, pmd, addr, &ptl);
>  	if (!start_pte)
> -		return 0;
> +		goto out;
>  	flush_tlb_batched_pending(mm);
>  	lazy_mmu_mode_enable();
>  	for (; addr < end; pte += nr, addr += nr * PAGE_SIZE) {
> @@ -568,6 +568,7 @@ static int madvise_cold_or_pageout_pte_range(pmd_t *pmd,
>  			folio_deactivate(folio);
>  	}
>
> +out:

Seems odd to put this here for a condition that explicitly guarantees
!start_pte? It should be before the if (pageout) reclaim_pages(...);
surely?

I honestly wonder whether, rather than adding yet another label/goto into this
absolute bloody mess, whether we should just live with a bit of duplication and do:

	if (!start_pte) {
		if (pageout)
			reclaim_pages(&folio_list);
		return 0;
	}

I actually think that'd be clearer at this point than throwing in some more
indirection.

That's for the backport but somebody needs to rework this entire bloody
function going forwards...

Cheers, Lorenzo

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/4] mm: support promotion-only NUMA hinting scans
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces support for promotion-only NUMA hinting scans in the Linux kernel. It adds a new flag MM_CP_PROT_NUMA_PROMO_ONLY to distinguish between placement and promotion-only scans, allowing the scanner to choose whether to promote pages or not. The change is made to the mm module, specifically in the functions change_prot_numa(), task_numa_work(), and vma_set_file(). The patch preserves existing behavior for certain fixes related to NUMA balancing and memory tiering systems.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/4] mm: allow shared folios to be promoted to a fast tier
series_items.patch_summary: This patch allows shared copy-on-write folios and executable file folios mapped by multiple processes to be promoted from a slow memory tier to a fast one, while maintaining existing restrictions for ordinary placement. This change is intended to improve the performance of memory tiering systems by allowing hot folios on slow tiers to be moved to faster storage. The patch modifies two kernel files, mm/mempolicy.c and mm/migrate.c, to relax the checks that previously blocked such promotions. The changes are based on a previous patch (c574bbe91703) that optimized page placement for memory tiering systems.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 3/4] sched/numa: scan read-only file mappings in tiering mode
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access) hinting mechanism to scan read-only file mappings when memory tiering is enabled, but only for promotion purposes. This change allows hot file folios on slow memory to be tracked by the tiering code, improving performance in certain scenarios. The patch addresses an issue where shared libraries and other read-only file-backed mappings were excluded from NUMA hinting, leading to placement bouncing and poor performance. By scanning these mappings, the patch enables more accurate tracking of runtime load and improves overall system responsiveness.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 4/4] sched/numa: do not let VMA PID activity gate promotion
series_items.patch_summary: This patch prevents VMA PID activity from gating memory promotion in NUMA-aware scheduling. It introduces a new field to track the sequence ID of socket-placement scans and allows periodic placement scans to avoid starvation. The change is motivated by a scenario where a large shmem VMA occupied each scan, causing 84 GB of VMAs to be skipped as inactive. The patch fixes a previous commit that enhanced vma scanning logic and improves memory tiering in multi-threaded applications.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/3] mm/huge_memory: make thp_underused() work for mTHP folios
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the thp_underused() function to make it work with mTHP folios, which are larger than PMD-sized folios. The function is made size-aware instead of hardcoded to PMD-sized folios. A new helper function, thp_can_be_underused(), is introduced to check if a folio can be underused based on the number of zero-filled pages and the sysctl maximum value. This change will allow anonymous mTHP folios to be added to the deferred split list in future patches.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/3] mm/huge_memory: don't queue folios that can never be underused
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the handling of anonymous PMD-sized folios in the Linux kernel by skipping the queuing of folios that can never be underused, reducing unnecessary work and improving performance. The default khugepaged/max_ptes_none setting causes the shrinker to never split these folios for being underused, so they are not queued. This change is particularly important for a subsequent patch that adds anonymous mTHP folios to the deferred split list, as it prevents small mTHP orders from taking the list_lru lock on every anonymous fault.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 3/3] mm/memory: add anonymous mTHP folios to the deferred split list
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds anonymous mTHP (huge page) folios to the deferred split list in the Linux kernel's memory management code. This allows for underused splitting of huge pages, which can help reclaim unused parts of large memory allocations when the system is under memory pressure. The patch addresses a problem where fully mapped huge pages that are mostly zero-filled do not get split by the deferred split shrinker, leading to memory regressions. The solution involves mirroring the behavior for PMD-sized folios and adding a check to minimize overhead on common fault paths.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses memory regressions caused by 2M THP=always on arm64 by splitting underused anonymous mTHP folios. The patches modify the deferred split shrinker to handle mTHP folios, which are not currently reclaimed when mostly zero-filled. Patch 1 makes thp_underused() folio-size aware, patch 2 keeps folios that can never be found underused off the queue, and patch 3 queues anonymous mTHP folios from map_anon_folio_pte_nopf(). The patches also adjust the behavior of khugepaged_max_ptes_none to make it an absolute count, rather than a per-folio order scaling factor.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH v2] fuse: enable large folios
patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch enables large folios in the FUSE (Filesystem in Userspace) kernel module. Large folios are a way to allocate memory in larger chunks, which can improve performance by reducing the number of requests made to the underlying storage device. The patch caps the maximum order at the largest request that FUSE can issue, ensuring that each folio fits within a single request. This approach allows the allocator to fall back to smaller folios under memory pressure. Benchmarks show significant improvements in read and write performance for both tmpfs backing and xfs on NVMe backing.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v1 1/3] virtio_fs: zero the correct range on a short read reply
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the virtio_fs module where it incorrectly zeroed the unfilled tail of a short read reply when the read started at an offset within a folio. The fix is to calculate the correct range to be zeroed based on the descriptor's offset and length, rather than relying on an assumption that only holds for small folios. This patch also removes a WARN_ON statement that was added as a diagnostic aid but is no longer needed. The change is necessary to enable support for large folios in virtio-fs.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v1 2/3] fuse: drop rather than zero the copied range in copy_file_range()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the fuse:copy_file_range() function to use invalidate_inode_pages2_range() instead of truncate_inode_pages_range(). The change is necessary because once file systems support folios larger than a page, truncate_inode_pages_range() can zero out parts of the copied range, leading to data loss. invalidate_inode_pages2_range() drops the entire folio without modifying its contents, which is more suitable for this use case. This patch aims to prevent data corruption and ensure correct behavior in scenarios where file systems support larger-than-page folios.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v1 3/3] fuse: replace folio_test_highmem() with folio_test_partial_kmap()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch replaces the use of folio_test_highmem() with folio_test_partial_kmap() in the fuse module's copy functionality. The change is necessary to ensure accurate handling of high memory mappings, particularly when using large folios and CONFIG_DEBUG_KMAP_LOCAL_FORCE_MAP is enabled. Without this change, fuse_copy_do() could copy past the end of a mapping on a highmem build with the mentioned configuration.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series prepares the Linux kernel for enabling large folios in the FUSE (Filesystem in Userspace) driver by updating several places that assume a folio is a single page or that a page-aligned range is also folio-aligned. The patches are based on previous work and do not change behavior until large folios are enabled, at which point they will become reachable. The series includes three patches: one for virtio-fs, one for FUSE's copy_file_range function, and one to replace an outdated memory test in the FUSE driver.

The patch corrects an issue where non-blocking allocations were being allowed access to HIGHATOMIC reserves, which can lead to performance problems and incorrect behavior. It introduces a new flag combination ALLOC_MASK_ATOMIC to represent atomic allocations, and updates the rmqueue_buddy function to use this flag correctly. This change ensures that only true atomic allocations are granted access to HIGHATOMIC reserves, preventing potential issues with other types of non-blocking allocations.

review_comments.author: Andrew Morton
review_comments.summary: Andrew Morton noted that the patch does not address all cases where GFP_NORETRY allocations are made, specifically mentioning GFP_NOWAIT and ~__GFP_DIRECT_RECLAIM sites, which do not get watermark exemptions and were not intended to be exempted by the original rmqueue_buddy() change.

v4:

From: Salvatore Dipietro <dipiets@amazon.it>
Subject: mm/page_alloc: avoid direct compaction for costly __GFP_NORETRY allocations
Date: Fri, 4 Sep 2026 11:56:28 +0000

Commit 5d8edfb900d5 ("iomap: Copy larger chunks from userspace")
introduced high-order folio allocations in the iomap buffered write path. 
When memory is fragmented, each failed costly-order allocation enters
__alloc_pages_slowpath() which runs direct compaction and
drain_all_pages(), causing a 0.38x throughput drop on PostgreSQL pgbench
(simple-update) with 1024 clients on a 96-vCPU arm64 system.

The root issue is that direct compaction is too expensive for hot
allocation paths that have fallbacks to smaller allocations. 
__filemap_get_folio_mpol() already marks higher-order allocations with
__GFP_NORETRY | __GFP_NOWARN, signalling that the caller can handle
failure.  However, the page allocator still attempts full direct
compaction for costly orders with __GFP_NORETRY, which is unnecessarily
aggressive when the caller will simply retry at a lower order.

For costly-order allocations with __GFP_NORETRY, clear
__GFP_DIRECT_RECLAIM at the very start of the slowpath, before
can_direct_reclaim, can_compact and the nofail checks are evaluated.  This
makes the entire slowpath treat the request as non-blocking: no direct
reclaim, no direct compaction and no drain_all_pages() IPI across every
CPU.  kswapd (and in turn kcompactd) is still woken further down for
background defragmentation, so compaction keeps working for long-term
system health while being removed from the latency-critical direct
allocation path.

Allocations that also request __GFP_THISNODE are exempted.  That flag
pairing identifies the local-node-first THP attempt issued by
alloc_pages_mpol() (mempolicy.c), which relies on direct compaction to
form transparent huge pages.

Test environment:
  Hardware:  AWS EC2 m8g.24xlarge (96 vCPU, arm64)
             12x 1TB IO2 32000 IOPS RAID0 XFS
  OS:        AL2023
  Kernel:    v7.3-rc1
  Database:  PostgreSQL 18.4
  Workload:  pgbench simple-update, 1024 clients, 96 threads, 1200s

Results (average of 3 runs, TPS):

  Config                   Avg TPS      % vs Baseline
  baseline (no patch)       59,408       -
  With this patch          155,409      +161.6%

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 1/5] mm/memcontrol: flatten try_charge_memcg control flow
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the try_charge_memcg function in the Linux kernel's memory control module to simplify its control flow by separating the logic for memsw and memory page counters into distinct paths.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 2/5] mm/page_counter: introduce per-CPU stock
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a per-CPU stock representation in the page_counter layer, mirroring the existing seven-slot representation from memcg. The new structure, struct page_counter_stock_pcp, preserves all fields and behaviors from its memcg equivalent but adds a backpointer to the base of the percpu stock. The patch also updates the page_counter structure to include pointers to the base of the percpu stock and the owning cgroup_subsys_state. No functional changes are intended in this initial introduction.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 3/5] mm/page_counter: make page_counter_try_charge() stock-aware
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the page_counter_try_charge() function to be aware of stock, allowing it to consume stock transparently while preserving existing semantics. Two new parameters are added: may_batch and nr_charged. The first parameter preserves the behavior of !allow_spinning scenarios in try_charge_memcg, where the goal is to charge as quickly as possible without evicting other stock slots or making a greedy charge to refill the stock. The second parameter reflects the size of the successful hierarchy charge, preserving existing batch-based memory.high accounting for current->memcg_nr_pages_over_high.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 4/5] mm/memcontrol: move memory stock to page counters
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the memory stock from memcg to page counters, allowing for more flexible management of memory usage. The change decouples the memory and memsw counters, which can temporarily diverge in value. To preserve the legacy user-visible invariant that memory usage is less than or equal to swap usage, the larger raw value between memory and memsw is reported. The patch also removes unused memcg code and preserves existing behaviors for cgroup v2 users. Future work will introduce additional page counters without removing the fast path.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 5/5] mm/memcontrol: add stock to the memsw page counter
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a separate stock to the memsw page counter, allowing it to operate independently of the memory bank. The common drain scheduling is factored into schedule_stock_drain(), and the existing direct memsw rollback is preserved when memory charge fails. This change enables the raw counters for both banks to temporarily drift due to cached amounts, while maintaining the user-visible cgroup-v1 invariant by reporting the larger value.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series moves the per-CPU cache of pre-charged pages, known as 'stock', from mem_cgroup to page_counter. This change is necessary to make future page_counters scalable and performant, particularly for scenarios where multiple new page_counters are introduced to a memcg. The patch simplifies try_charge_memcg code and preserves existing draining, refilling, and uncharging behavior. For memcg v1 users, the decoupling of memory and memsw stocks may lead to different precharged cache sizes, but this is addressed by reporting the larger value of usage_in_bytes for memsw reporting.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 01/12] mm/khugepaged: drop redundant mm_struct pin in madvise_collapse()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch removes an unnecessary mmgrab() reference in the madvise_collapse() function, which is already holding a valid mm_users reference. The redundant mmgrab() was being held across the work of madvise_collapse(), but since all callers to this function already hold a valid reference to the mm_struct, it can be safely dropped. This patch simplifies the code and reduces unnecessary memory management.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 02/12] mm/khugepaged: count collapses where khugepaged makes them
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the khugepaged functionality to count collapses where it makes them, allowing the daemon to keep its own counter without relying on shared paths. The change affects the collapse_single_pmd function, which now increments the khugepaged_pages_collapsed counter only when the caller is the khugepaged daemon and the collapse is successful.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 03/12] mm/khugepaged: rename mthp_present_ptes bitmap to eligible_ptes
series_items.patch_summary: This patch renames the 'mthp_present_ptes' bitmap in the khugepaged code to 'eligible_ptes'. The name change reflects that a set bit in this bitmap indicates not only that a PTE is present, but also that it has passed additional checks such as uffd, lazyfree, anonymity, and sharing. The patch updates comments and code accordingly without introducing any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 04/12] mm/collapse: add collapse.h for the collapse interface
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new header file, mm/collapse.h, to separate the interface and state of the collapse mechanism from its implementation in khugepaged.c. The new header defines an enum for scan results and a struct for control data passed between the user and engine sides. Two constants are also moved from khugepaged.c to the new header. This change improves code organization and maintainability without introducing any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 05/12] mm/collapse: state what a collapse may do in the policy
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new struct collapse_policy that allows the caller to specify what actions are allowed during a memory collapse operation. The policy is used by khugepaged and MADV_COLLAPSE to determine which VMAs are eligible for collapse, how many empty or swapped-out PTEs can be included in a window, and other settings. The patch removes the need for the collapse code to look up who called it and instead relies on the caller to fill in the policy once per scan pass or call. This change simplifies the code and improves performance by reducing the number of checks performed during each table scan.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 06/12] mm/collapse: drop the collapse_possible() wrapper
series_items.patch_summary: This patch removes the collapse_possible() function wrapper, which only forwarded to collapse_possible_orders(). The three callers of collapse_possible() can directly test the mask returned by collapse_possible_orders(), resulting in no functional change.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 07/12] mm/collapse: name the per-table scan reset for what it resets
series_items.patch_summary: This patch renames the function collapse_control_init_scan() to collapse_scan_reset(), which more accurately reflects its purpose of resetting accumulated data for a scan, including node load, allocation nodemask, and eligible PTE bitmap. This change is part of a larger effort to improve naming conventions in the code and prepare for future changes that will involve initialization and release functions for each control. The patch does not introduce any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 08/12] mm/collapse: separate scanning a PTE table from collapsing it
series_items.patch_summary: This patch separates the scanning of a PTE table from its collapse into two distinct functions: `collapse_scan_pmd` and `collapse_run_pmd`. The scan function reads the PTE table under the mmap_lock, while the run function performs the actual collapse. This change improves code organization and reduces the complexity of the original `collapse_single_pmd` function.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 09/12] mm/collapse: open-code collapse_single_pmd() in its two callers
series_items.patch_summary: This patch removes the function collapse_single_pmd() and instead open-codes its functionality in two callers, khugepaged's lock_dropped and madvise_collapse(). The original function had a complex locking contract that is simplified by having each caller drop and reacquire the necessary locks. This change does not introduce any functional changes but rather simplifies the code and improves maintainability.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 10/12] mm/collapse: work out the orders a VMA allows once per VMA
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the way VMA (Virtual Memory Area) orders are calculated by only doing it once per VMA instead of once per PTE table. This is done to improve performance and reduce unnecessary work. The patch also introduces a new parameter, `enabled_orders`, which is passed from the caller to the function that calculates the allowed orders for a VMA. This change allows the code to take advantage of the fact that hugepage_vma_revalidate() tests the order again under the lock the collapse retakes, making it more efficient.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 11/12] mm/collapse: declare the collapse interface in collapse.h
series_items.patch_summary: This patch declares the collapse interface in collapse.h, which includes functions and variables related to collapsing memory pages. The functions are: collapse_control_init, collapse_scan_pmd, collapse_run_pmd, and collapse_control_release. These functions are used for collapsing large pages into smaller ones. The patch also renames hugepage_vma_revalidate to collapse_vma_revalidate and adds comments to explain the order of function calls and lock usage. This is a preparation step for implementing MADV_COLLAPSE in madvise.c, but it does not introduce any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 12/12] mm/collapse: implement MADV_COLLAPSE in madvise.c
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the implementation of MADV_COLLAPSE from khugepaged.c to madvise.c, where it belongs among other madvise operations. This change simplifies the code and removes unnecessary dependencies between the daemon's file and the syscall code. The MADV_COLLAPSE operation is a caller of the interface used by khugepaged, so its functionality remains unchanged. Additionally, the !CONFIG_TRANSPARENT_HUGEPAGE stub is moved along with the implementation.

This separation allows for better modularity and maintainability of the code, as well as improved handling of lock states and policy decisions. From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>

khugepaged.c holds both the users of collapse and the machinery that
performs it.  The daemon's scan loop, the sysfs tunables, MADV_COLLAPSE's
entry point and the collapse itself all sit in one file and reach into
each other freely.  Nothing marks where a user ends and the engine
begins.

Start drawing that line.

Add mm/collapse.h for what the two sides have to agree on:

  - enum scan_result - what the engine hands back;
  - struct collapse_control - the state a request carries.

And two constants move with them:

  - KHUGEPAGED_MAX_PTES_LIMIT -> COLLAPSE_MAX_PTES_LIMIT;
  - KHUGEPAGED_MIN_MTHP_ORDER -> COLLAPSE_MIN_MTHP_ORDER.

Neither is a fact about the daemon, so both lose the KHUGEPAGED_ prefix.

No functional change.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 1/5] mm: let folio_mkclean() report which pages had dirty PTEs
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the folio_mkclean() function to report which pages had dirty PTEs by introducing a new function, folio_mkclean_dirtymap(). The latter takes a bitmap and sets a bit for every page of the folio whose entry was dirty. The original folio_mkclean() function is now a wrapper that passes no bitmap, preserving its existing behavior. This change allows downstream code to track which parts of a large folio were written through a mapping, rather than assuming the whole folio changed.

review_comments.author: Usama Arif
review_comments.summary: Reviewer noted that holding the page-table lock prevents another kernel thread from changing the PTE, but does not prevent the CPU from setting the hardware dirty bit, leading to a timing window where the bitmap is populated from an outdated snapshot of the PTEs. This issue arises in range-aware iomap writeback scenarios and can result in incorrect final dirty state.
review_comments.raw_body:
The patch reads the PTE first and then records pte_dirty(entry) in the bitmap
before invalidating the PTE.

Holding the page-table lock prevents another kernel thread from changing
the PTE, but it does not prevent the CPU from setting the hardware dirty
bit.

This sequence is possible:

  Writeback CPU                  Application CPU
  -------------                  ---------------
  ptep_get(): writable, clean
                                 store through the PTE
                                 hardware sets dirty
  ptep_clear_flush(): returns dirty PTE
  pte_mkclean()
  reinstall clean, read-only PTE

The bitmap was populated from the first, clean snapshot. The dirty state
returned by ptep_clear_flush() is discarded.

With range-aware iomap writeback:

- The folio can still be selected for writeback.
- The affected filesystem block is absent from the iomap dirty bitmap.
- Writeback clears the folio dirty state without writing that block.
- Later eviction can discard the modified data.

The old whole-folio behavior did not need to know which PTE became
dirty, so this timing window was harmless. Sub-folio tracking makes the
final dirty state correctness-critical.

The PMD path has the identical race between pmdp_get() and
pmdp_invalidate().

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 2/5] mm: add a_ops->dirty_folio_range() and use the mkclean dirty harvest
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new operation to the address_space_operations structure called dirty_folio_range(), which allows filesystems to mark specific ranges of a folio as dirty instead of the entire folio. It also introduces a new function folio_mark_dirty_range() that uses this new operation. The patch then updates the folio_clear_dirty_for_io() function to use folio_mkclean_dirtymap() and hand the dirty ranges to the filesystem, reducing unnecessary writes in cases where only part of a folio is modified.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 3/5] mm: keep the mmap dirty range down to the faulting page
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the way the Linux kernel handles dirty ranges in memory mappings. It reduces the dirty range to a single page when only that page is written, rather than marking the entire folio as dirty. This change improves performance by avoiding unnecessary work and reducing the number of faults that occur due to incorrect dirty state. The patch addresses two specific issues: one where a shared mapping's folio was being marked dirty unnecessarily, and another where a batch of pages was being marked dirty on a write fault, even if only some of those pages were actually written to. The change is made in the `fault_dirty_shared_page` and `set_pte_range` functions, which are responsible for handling faults and page table updates.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 4/5] iomap: narrow page_mkwrite() dirtying to the faulting page
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the iomap code to narrow page_mkwrite() dirtying to only the faulting page, rather than the entire folio. It introduces a new function iomap_dirty_folio_range() that allows for more precise control over which parts of a folio are marked as dirty. The buffered write path and the mmap path now set the dirty range differently, with the latter setting everything due to the whole-folio coverage by iomap_dirty_folio(). The patch also updates several functions to use the new function and corrects some inconsistencies in the code.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 5/5] xfs: track mmap dirty state per block
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the XFS file system to track the dirty state of memory-mapped blocks individually, rather than at the folio (2M) level. This change is made possible by replacing the `dirty_folio` operation with a new `dirty_folio_range` operation that allows for more precise tracking of dirty blocks. As a result, when writing data to a shared mapping, only the affected block is written back instead of the entire folio.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch set introduces sub-folio dirty tracking for PTE-mapped mmap writes, addressing the issue of large page cache folios being dirtied unnecessarily when a single byte is written through a shared file mapping. The problem arises because current implementations mark the entire folio as dirty, leading to inefficient writeback and increased minor fault counts. To solve this, the patch harvests hardware PTE dirty bits at page_mkwrite() time and provides the filesystem with the ranges that were actually modified, allowing for more targeted writeback. This approach is already implemented in XFS and is shown to reduce writeback by 99% on a large file system.

review_comments.raw_body:
It is always called, but once per folio, not once per page. It is the
filesystem's chance to preallocate whatever it needs to track dirty
state for the *folio*.

Later finish_fault() maps the folio. It tries to map it fully when it
can, so a write fault creates up to 512 writable PTEs on x86. And we
really do need to map the folio fully whenever we can. Otherwise we
significantly undercount mlocked memory. See commit 19773df031bc
("mm/fault: try to map the entire file folio in finish_fault()").

the dirtying to a subset of pages. Any of them can turn dirty at any

review_comments.summary: Reviewer Kiryl Shutsemau agrees to remove the ->dirty_folio() function, which makes little sense, and instead proposes bundling dirtying into ->page_mkwrite(). He suggests that this distinction between making a folio writable and marking it dirty is meaningful, allowing filesystems to provide fine-grained dirty tracking through ->dirty_folio_range().
review_comments.raw_body:
Boris pointed me to Matthew's proposal to remove ->dirty_folio:

https://lore.kernel.org/all/aoyWln-Gt-yvZQkE@casper.infradead.org

I agree that the current ->dirty_folio() makes little sense and that
dirtying the folio can be bundled into ->page_mkwrite(), as they are
matched 1-to-1.

My proposal makes the distinction between making the folio writable and
making it dirty meaningful. ->page_mkwrite() allocates whatever is needed
on the filesystem side to track dirty state and drive writeback for the
*folio*, while ->dirty_folio_range() marks part of the folio dirty.

We can still drop ->dirty_folio(). A filesystem can provide
->dirty_folio_range() if it wants fine-grained (sub-folio) dirty
tracking.

A separate question is whether we want to avoid installing a writable PMD
entry for filesystems that want fine-grained dirty tracking. I have a
patch for this, but it deserves a separate discussion once we agree that we
want this for PTE-mapped folios first.
